utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Okay. [Interpretation] "I told her then that we could not arrest Sreten Lukic not out of the fear of the reaction of the police or the public but because I, in January 2001, when the checks were made with the Western governments and their intelligence services, including the ICTY, and the reply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's sufficient. Thank you. No doubt Mr. Lukic may try a bit more to clarify this. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will attempt to clarify that, Your Honour. I think that you started to explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you were saying this to Carla Del Ponte, did you have in mind the conclusions from the bodies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't answer that. Please, Mr. Lukic, no leading questions in re-examination. We've already had your examination of the evidence weakened a little in re-examination by the nature of -- or the introduction to that question about the reason for not arresting Lukic. And this is the same topic, it's a very important one. So open questions only, please, otherwise the answer will not be of assistance to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you replied to Mrs. Del Ponte, what did you have in mind when you said this to her?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: The conversation with Mrs. Del Ponte took place on the 20th of October, 2003. I have told you what I said to her at the time and what were my reasons for believing that we would not be able to extradite Lukic. The conclusion of the government was adopted on the 23rd of October. That is to say, three days later. And the conclusion of the government was not my formulation, no. It was a proposal submitted by the Ministry of the Interior which I supported, naturally, but there is this difference. The ministry gave the formal reasons why Lukic could not be extradited. The law defining the cooperation with The Hague Tribunal, I think in Article 6, states that the council of ministers of the state union, that is to say the governments of the member republics, when establishing that cooperation would endanger the security in the country could alert The Hague Tribunal about that, and it was based on that that the government conclusion was adopted. Naturally the indictment against Lukic unsettled both the police and the public, and those were two legitimate reasons for that conclusion, but in addition to them there is this additional reason which I pointed out back on the 20th of October, that reason being that after all the checks had been made the Tribunal clearly stated that there was no investigation pending against Lukic. In the almost three years from the time when a decision was made on appointing Lukic until the 20th of October, 2003, Carla Del Ponte, even though she met with a lot of people in Serbia at some 15 meetings, never uttered any complaint or objection about the fact that Lukic was appointed to that position. The fact that that indictment was issued on the 2nd of October looked like something that was done in hindsight, because Lukic would not have been appointed to that position had we been told that there was a investigation pending against him. In addition to other high officials of MUP were inquired about, and we were told about all three of them that no investigation was pending against them. Therefore, under the circumstances it was quite natural for us to appoint him as a professional to that position, and it was quite abnormal for the Chief Prosecutor to come three years later and to say that he had been indicted when nothing had changed in the meantime in terms of the facts that were available to her. Because I asked her what had changed in these three years, and she told me he was chief of police in Kosovo in 1998. And I told her, "Well, I know that. The whole world knows that, and you knew that back in 2001 when you told us that no investigation was spending against him."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zivkovic, we will now turn to another topic. You spoke about establishing a working group or a task force.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 6D91 brought up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, before of we proceed down this avenue, perhaps he can tell us what the purpose of it is. Is it something that arose in cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The issue of who actually established it was raised by you, and the exact role of Mr. Lukic was raised by you, and if that can be clarified then that would be of assistance to us. If it requires reference to a document and that somehow or other prejudices you, you will be given another opportunity to come back on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zivkovic, a question was put to you about who had formally established this task force, and we here have an announcement, a communique, a public announcement that was made by the MUP of Serbia, a press release. Did you know at the time that the chief of the public security sector, and it was Mr. Lukic at the time in that office.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's surely going to be another leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm asking if he was aware at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just please no exchanges across the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. I'm just trying to be clear about this point. Mr. Stamp, I missed your intervention, as did the court reporter. What was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was referring to the formulation of the question and indicating that it certainly appeared to be a leading question or the beginnings of a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think for once it's not one that's going to cause any significant damage. But it's dangerous territory, Mr. Lukic, to be prompting the witness unless it's a pure formality. It looks as though at the moment that's what is involved in this instance, but please be cautious in case the evidence that results is devalued.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What I wanted to ask this witness, Your Honour, is whether he was aware of the real force behind this working group. If he wasn't aware at the time, then I would be satisfied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but putting this press release and then stating his position and so on doesn't help you to get a clear piece of evidence that's plainly from his recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move on, Mr. Zivkovic, and I'm drawing my re-examination to an end. In answer to Prosecutor's question on page 50, line 21, you spoke about the release of Milan Lukic from custody. At that time were you aware of the fact, or are you aware of that fact today, that Milan Lukic was released from custody by the police or the investigating judge? Who was it? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: It's a self-evident question. It is the investigating judge who remands a person in custody and releases that same person. It is the technical service of the prison who obviously releases the person but it is the investigating judge who releases the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivkovic, for testifying on behalf of Mr. Sreten Lukic's defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry I have to intervene. Page 68, line 3. It says it is the technical service of the prison who obviously releases the person, but it is the investigating judge who releases the order. I think that the witness mentioned police as a technical service in this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you explain again, Mr. Zivkovic, what you said? You said it was self-evident who released Milan Lukic and any other accused. Could you explain the roles again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. An order is issued by the investigating judge for a person to be remanded in custody. And then the investigating judge again issues a decision to release the person, but the decision is implemented by the police. The police is in charge of bringing the person in and releasing the person. When it comes to the decision on remanding the person in custody and on the term of that remand in custody it is up to the investigating judge to decide that. In other words, it is not the police that may decide on who will be kept in prison and for how long.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, 68, 20. The police is in charge of bringing the person in, in, and releasing the person, it's absolutely not correct, and that's not what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what do you say he said?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The police has nothing to do with releasing the person, any person from the prison, and prison is not under the police at all. It's under the Ministry of Justice and police has nothing to do with prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Zivkovic, we have an English statement from you on the transcript that the police is in charge of bringing the person in and releasing the person. Is that an accurate translation of what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said it is the investigating judge who issues an order on remanding a person in custody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We know that. All we're interested in is what you said about the practical implementation of that order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I said explicitly that the police cannot release anybody from prison. That's on the one. On the two, the police on the order of the Judge arrests a person and brings them to prison, but they don't release the person from the prison. A person may be released from prison upon the decision of the investigating judge, and the police has nothing whatsoever to do with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So who physically deals with the release of the person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the person is in custody the physical release is carried out by the guards of the prison upon the -- the order of the investigating judge, and the guards are part of the Ministry of Justice, not of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Anything further, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivkovic. That completes your evidence. Thank you for coming here to give evidence. You may now leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Our next witness is Mr. Dragan Furdulovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Furdulovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You will now be examined by Mr. Ivetic on behalf of Mr. Lukic. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Furdulovic. Mr. Furdulovic, did you give a written statement to the members of the Defence team of Sreten Lukic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could ask the usher's assistance I have a hard copy of that statement which is 6D1605 which I would ask also to be pulled up on e-court. And, sir, once you receive this document, I would merely ask you to review the same and tell us if this is in fact the written statement that you tendered to the Defence team of Sreten Lukic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if I could first of all direct your attention to paragraph 1 of the statement. Do you have any revisions or clarifications with respect to this paragraph of the statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm currently an advisor to the assistant of the minister and chief of department of interior control with the police, and my occupation is the main police advisor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, if we could move on to the next paragraph. Do you have any clarifications or corrections with respect to that paragraph of this written statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the second paragraph I would like to correct the following: The date when I was transferred from the position of the chief of the department of market inspection in the ministry, instead of 1997, it should read 2000. The year should be 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now this is an item for which -- well, if we look at -- if we look at paragraph 8, in the last sentence of the English translation of paragraph 8 of your statement, the abbreviation or acronym CZ is said to stand for the central gaol. Is that in fact what you intended to mean here by using the acronym CZ?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: The abbreviations CZ stands for the workers of the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now if we could turn to paragraph 10 of the statement. Do you have any directions or clarifications with respect to that paragraph of this written statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the sentence which reads: "At that time I reported directly," after the word "reported" a word should be added and that word should read "The Prosecutor."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, apart from the correction cited today, does this written statement accurately reflect your words as given to the members of the Lukic Defence team on these topics?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if I were to ask you questions today on these same topics under oath, would your answers be the same as those reflected in this written statement subject to the corrections that you've made here today?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would at this time move for Exhibit 6D1605 the written statement of Mr. Furdulovic to be accepted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, I would like to pose some additional questions of you relating to the topics of your statement and otherwise. First of all, if you could look at paragraph 8 of the same, which I think was on the previous page in the B/C/S, and the measures undertaken by the MUP of Serbia following the discovery of the ID documents for the Berisa family during the 2001 Batajnica examinations and particularly the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic is kindly requested to slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, sorry, high speed in ordinary circumstances is to be encouraged. Here, if you can just slow a little and go into seventh gear.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will do my best, Your Honour. You know I sometimes have difficulty doing that, especially if I'm reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could begin again, sir. At paragraph 8 of your statement, and in particular where you describe the measures undertaken by the MUP of Serbia to uncover the crime of murder against the Berisa family following the discovery of ID documents during the 2001 Batajnica exhumations, and the question I have for you is how would you describe Sreten Lukic's activities relative to this MUP investigation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: The role of Sreten Lukic as the chief of the public security sector in this concrete case reflected in his constant agreement to approve interviews with all members of the security sector for whom we believed as a task force that interviews should be conducted and information collected in view of revealing details of the Berisa family murder. At the same time, the role of Sreten Lukic was to enable us an insight into the complete documentation that might be of use to us in our further police investigation and especially documents issued by the Krusevac SUP, the Prizren SUP of the Suva Reka police OUP. His role was also to provide logistical support in this case and in all the other cases, all the logistical support that we needed in order to carry out certain operative actions in a timely and efficient fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if -- if we could take a moment to call up Exhibit 6D1608. And while we're waiting for that document to come up on the screen, sir, I would ask the question that you will have to consider once the document comes up and that is if you recognise this document and what can you tell us in relation to this document that is now up on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I recognise the document. This is a document issued by the administration for fighting organised crime that I compiled on the 22nd of March, 2002. In the left corner you can see my initials, DF. The document was sent to the assistant minister, to General Colonel Sreten Lukic, head of the public security sector. In this document we inform him that we act upon the order of the Prosecutor in Belgrade and that we collect information in order to reveal the details of the Berisa family murder. We hereby ask for his approval to approve interview with Radojko Repanovic, the commander of the police station in Suva Reka at a certain time, all in accordance with our plan of activities. In the left lower corner we see the signature of the chief of my administration given that I was at the time a member of the department for fighting organised crime with the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And we see the name Sreten Lukic and a signature in the upper right. What did this part of the document mean, technically speaking, or in an authoritative sense to you in terms of your investigation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: This was a customary way of addressing the chief of sector when we sought approval to interview all members of the sector regardless of their rank, position, and duties they were involved in. We see that General Sreten Lukic signed the document personally, and his signature meant for us that we could carry out interviews with the aforementioned policemen without any obstructions. And it is also the signal to the policemen that he had to reply to our invitation and to come for this interview at the given time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Furdulovic. I apologise for the pause. I'm just waiting for the translation and the transcript to catch up to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see we're also at the point for the last break. If it assists the Court and the translators, we could do that at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Furdulovic, we have to have a break at this stage. That will be for half an hour. Would you please leave the courtroom with the usher and we'll see you again at 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Furdulovic, before the break we were looking at 6D1608, which is still up on the screen, relating to the request for an informative conversation with Repanovic Radojko. Did you in fact as part of your investigation conduct such an informative conversation or interview with the named person and if so to whom would the results of that -- of that conversation have been sent?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: We conducted the interview at a different time with Radojko Repanovic. We took his statement and recorded it, and we forwarded this record of the statement to the district public prosecutor in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just waiting for the translation and transcript again, sir. Did you take point in time have to inform Assistant Minister Lukic or ask for his further permission or authorisation to forward the gathered material to the appropriate prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at 6D1609, and if I can ask you to review this document and tell us if you recognise the same and what you can tell us about the circumstances of this document.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: Again, this is a document issued by the administration for fighting organised crime. It was drafted in March 2002 by myself personally, which is confirmed by my initials, DF. It was sent to General Lukic as the head of the public security sector. He is hereby informed that we are acting upon the public prosecutor in order to elucidate the murder of the Berisa family, and we're asking for his consent for an interview to be conducted with a policeman Ramiz Papic from the Sjenica OUP. In the right upper corner I notice the signature of General Lukic showing that he gave us his consent to interview the aforementioned policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And again did you in fact proceed with the conduct of an informative discussion or interview, and did you send those results off to some other entity or body?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: We took Ramiz Papic's statement and recorded it, and we forwarded the record of that statement to the prosecutor in Belgrade, to the district public prosecutor in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Document related to this investigation as a sample. If we could look at 6D1610, dated November of 2002. Is this tied to the same investigation, and is this document one that came about in a similar procedure as you've described for the previous two documents?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is about the murder of the Berisa family. Again General Lukic's consent was requested and received to carry out interviews with four members of the public security sector. Those were all officers, one a captain, another lieutenant, a colonel lieutenant, and a warrant officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us in total how many persons you conducted such informative interviews with and how many statements you recorded in the matter before forwarding the same to the prosecutors in the Berisa case for the murder that occurred in Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: In total we interviewed 38 persons as a result of which we had 44 records and statements. We took a statement of each and every one of them but with a number of policemen we had several interviews. All the statements that were recorded were forwarded to the district public prosecutor in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you mentioned you talked with a number of individuals and a number of policemen. Was every -- did -- strike that. Were any requests for your investigation to speak with any members of the RJB ever declined by Sreten Lukic? Was consent ever declined for any individual that was the -- a person of interest to speak with as part of your investigation in this particular proceeding?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: Whenever we issued a request to interview any member of the public security sector we received Mr. Lukic's consent to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And before moving on, was the scope and extent of your investigation limited to just interviewing policemen?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: Within the scope of our planned activities leading to the elucidation of the crime we interviewed about 25 policemen, if my memory serves me right. One of -- member of the sector of public security, a number of citizens, civilians, and a number of members of the civilian protection. So these were the people that we interviewed within the scope of that investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, is that an accurate reflection of that answer in line 14, one member of the sector of public security?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: State security I believe is what the witness said. We can -- let me just ask him. Might as well ask him to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, you're recorded as saying that one member of the sector of public security was interviewed. Am I correct -- well, is that what you said and can you clarify that for us? Who in fact is the one individual from the specific sector that was interviewed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said that for all the members of the public security sector we received consent from General Lukic. When we drafted a total of 44 interviews, we had an interview by Milorad Nisovic who was the state security sector member. This is the first document that pointed to certain facts with regard to this crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to that state security member, was that -- strike that. With respect to the state security member, would the request for an interview have been submitted to Mr. Lukic as head of the RJB or to someone else?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: No. Mr. Lukic did not receive our request to interview this member of the state security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know how long was this investigation period approximately, and how did Mr. Lukic act towards the investigation? That is to say, did he hinder it in any way?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: Our police investigation lasted from the moment when the mass grave in Batajnica was opened and when a certain number of ID documents were found on the 36 exhumed bodies. That was in 2001. And the investigation lasted until the year 2003. Not for a single moment did General Lukic hinder our plans. Whenever we had a request for an interview, he would give his consent, and he would also allow us to take over documents that we were interested in that were in the possession of any of the units of the public security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we can move along then. In paragraph 10 you discussed the Bitiqi matter, and you're recorded as using the terminology: "His policemen." Could you explain what you meant by that term?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: In the police jargon his policemen or my policemen means that either I, or him in this case, were these policemens' supervising officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In reference to the time period when the investigation was ongoing or to some other time period?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: It refers to the time period of the investigation, when the investigation was conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could look at 6D1611. If you could take a moment to look at this document and let us know if this document is known to you and what additional comments you can make on the same, particularly if in fact in the Bitiqi case the same procedure that you've described for us here was followed with respect to conducting the investigation and seeking and receiving consent from the head of the RJB, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: This document issued by the department fighting organised crime shows a similar principle of addressing General Lukic in order to seek his consent to carry out certain actions in order to elucidate the brothers Bitiqi murders. We asked for his consent to carry out interviews of six policemen of whom some were high-ranking officers of the MUP, in high positions at the time. For example, the deputy chief of the police administration, lieutenant general, the commander of the Gendarmerie, the chief of the Prokuplje SUP, the chief of training in the command of the Gendarmerie and also in the right-hand side could I see the signature of General Lukic giving us his consent to carry out interviews with the aforementioned policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in the course of the investigation into this matter as conducted by your element of the MUP, did you experience or witness any obstruction on the part of Sreten Lukic with regards to this investigation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: We were not obstructed by General Lukic in any of the phases of our investigation work.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, in addition to the activities we have thus far been discussing and which are also -- go further in your statement, did the MUP also undertake any activities relative to witnesses or victims for these any of these investigations based on the request of judicial organs during the tenure of Sreten Lukic as head of the RJB?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: We had several requests in the course of our police investigation to extend particular measures of protection to certain individuals. One of them came from District Court in Belgrade, which -- and there was also a request from the fund for humanitarian law to provide particular measures for seven witnesses and peoples who suffered damages in Podujevo in 1997 when about 19 citizens had been killed. Before the District Court in Belgrade there was an investigation against -- against Sasa Cvejtan and we were requested to provide special security measures from the entry of persons from (redacted) into the territory of Serbia during their testimony before the court, during their stay in the district prison where the line-up was organised and until the moment when these persons left the territory of Serbia. We had special requests from the fund for humanitarian rights in order to carry out these special measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And how would you describe the role of Mr. Lukic with respect to these requests for providing these security measures for the witnesses who were coming for this criminal proceeding?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: The application of special security measures meant that these persons, from the moment they crossed into the territory of Serbia were provided special protection measures. For that portion the border police was in charge and that was an organisational unit within the public security sector. That is -- it is well known that General Lukic was the chief of the public security sector. None of these measures could have been implemented without his direct approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, with regard to all of the foregoing investigations that we have discussed here orally and the investigations that are -- that are set forth also in your written statement, did you ever come across any credible information tending to suggest that Sreten Lukic was involved in either war crimes or the covering up of war crimes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: I was involved in investigations from May 2001 until the 1st of February, 2004, when I assumed a different position, and I never heard nor did I ever receive any kind of information indicating that Sreten Lukic took part in any way in any war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we can move on to a different but related topic. In the course of your work in performing investigations as we have discussed here, did you have occasion to personally be involved in any informative talks or interviews of a person -- of a policeman by the name of Bozidar Protic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I conducted an interview with him together with my chief head of the task force, Captain Dragan Karleusa, and on the orders of Mr. Karleusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And -- sorry, just waiting for the transcript again. Based on your personal knowledge how many times did you or someone from your service undertake to talk or interview Mr. Protic regarding his knowledge of the mass graves and the matters arising therefrom?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: We conducted an interview with Mr. Protic several times. I remember that in June we talked to him at least five times. I interviewed him together with Captain Karleusa. As far as I remember, we drafted one Official Note dated the 4th of June, 2001. The reason why Official Notes were not drawn following each interview was that Mr. Protic frequently gave confused and incomplete statements. He kept changing certain information. He couldn't recollect how the corpses were brought in, using what routes. He was dissatisfied with his son's situation because he was employed. He was also dissatisfied with his housing, which wasn't resolved. In addition to that, in 2002 I had occasion as chief of the operations team of MUP to organise an interview with Bozidar Protic and to tell him that the OTP investigators would interview him. And also there was a summons from the District Court in Belgrade. That is to say we told him that he was -- it was his duty to respond to the summons and provide a statement, even though he kept evading that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can ask you to clarify one point. You're recorded at page 83, lines 14 through 16, of the statement as saying that Mr. Protic frequently gave confused and incomplete statements. He kept changing certain information. Was there in fact even -- strike that. Were there -- were there occasions when the information given by Mr. Protic, when checked, was found to be incorrect?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is not a proper question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry. It's a leading question. That is just answering the question in the way it is put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm asking the witness to -- I believe I have a basis for asking further question for -- asking for particular circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is a leading question. It's very easy to ask a much more general and open question about the information. So we will sustain that objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to check -- well, did you have occasion to check any of the information provided by Mr. Protic in the course of your interviews through independent means?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: I wish to reiterate that we did not speak with Mr. Protic until June of 2001, whereas our activities had begun on the 8th of May, 2001. That means that Bozidar Protic was not the only source of our investigative work. We did not always rely on his information. In fact, I remember that on the 14th of June, I personally opened the mass grave in Petrovo Selo. Protic was with me, as was the Prosecutor and investigative judge. We used machinery, and Protic could not remember the exact location of the pits. We tried to locate the pit several times and finally succeeded. In our view, he on that occasion proved once again that he wasn't a reliable source of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the course of your discussions with Mr. Protic, did he at any time ever mention Mr. Sreten Lukic in any sense or regard as to mass graves or to the transport of bodies from Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you highlight for us any differences or any unique nature of your activities as a working group in the period before the implementation of any law regulating cooperation with the ICTY and the relevant state organs with jurisdiction over such matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just object to this question for vagueness. One cannot ascertain having a look at this question whether or not it is intended to elicit evidence which is relevant to the issues before the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if I ask a more specific question I'd be leading, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm having difficulty understanding the question, Mr. Ivetic. Try again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you highlight for us, sir -- now, let me back up. Do you know, sir, when the law regulating cooperation with the ICTY entered into force on the territory of the -- I believe it was then a state union of Serbia and Montenegro, including the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: In April of 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And -- and based upon your testimony you've -- some of the investigative work that you performed pre-dated that. Could you highlight for us the bases for your investigative work prior to the entering into force of the law on cooperation with the ICTY? That is to say, was there cooperation with the ICTY on behalf of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia prior to this law entering into full force and effect?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: Our activities aimed at investigating war crimes commenced with the establishment of the working group on the 8th of May, 2001. We worked on a certain number of cases based on a specific task that was given to us in the decision issued by the minister, based on our own initiative at the request of the competent prosecutors and courts. The working group in the beginning encountered a number of problems. However, once the law on cooperation with The Hague Tribunal was adopted in 2002 as well as the law on organisation and competence of state organs in the proceedings concerning war crimes which was in 2003, our work entered the second phase, because these laws regulated the duty both of individuals and state organs concerning provision of available documentation and responding to summons and giving statements regardless of the capacity in which they did so. As for the duty which was regulated by the law on cooperation with the Hague Tribunal, we implemented that by establishing an operations team at the level of the ministry. It is from that time that direct cooperation was established with the Tribunal's office in Belgrade, and from that time on it was our priority to respond as quickly as possible to any requests given by The Hague Tribunal. In the first period of time when we functioned as a working group until these laws were passed, we had unlimited support of the Minister of the Interior Mr. Mihajlovic, chief of public security sector General Lukic, and other officials from the ministry, which came to be appointed after democratic changes in 2001. The result of our work in this first period of time was that our cases were tried before the judiciary, and a huge hindrance to us and to our work was that we could not conduct police investigations in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija even though at that time we had already established cooperation with UNMIK. We had had several meetings where we exchanged information concerning particular events. However, at that time that cooperation did not yield any results. In that period of time, we had particularly good contacts with Dejan Mihov, head of the ICTY office in Belgrade, who received from us information about all of the requests sent to The Hague Tribunal and received from them. We informed Dejan Mihov about all of that, and he was quite happy with our work at the time and said so publicly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Furdulovic, for your time. I have no further questions in direct examination for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. You'll now be cross-examined, Mr. Furdulovic, by the Prosecutor Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who first told you about the mass grave at Batajnica, or told the working group about the mass graves at Batajnica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: The information on Batajnica was conveyed to me by my boss, Captain Dragan Karleusa. I was given a task by him to go to Kladovo. And I don't know who gave that information to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And do you know how the working group came to be aware that there were pits with corpses in Petrovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: From the 12th until the 15th of May I personally interviewed more than 30 individuals in the territory of Negotin and Kladovo. We wrote about 23 Official Notes. Based on those interviews, we obtained information indicating that corpses had been transported. As for the particular information about the pit in Petrovo Selo, that was provided by Bozidar Protic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you interview any other drivers or people who transported bodies from Kosovo to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who were the other drivers who transported from Kosovo to Serbia that you interviewed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We talked to other drivers as well. I remember now that we talked to the driver called Ursuljanovic. I believe that he was the driver of the chief of the Bor SUP, Golubovic. I can't remember other names because it's ban long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did -- is the name that you gave us Ursuljanovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you take a statement from him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That statement is part of the work product of the task force that you were part of?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where did he take bodies from according to his statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: I can't give you any details about what he provided in his statement, but as far as I remember, he took the truck with corpses from Tekija towards Belgrade to Batajnica specifically. That's all I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So he took a truck, according to the information he gave you, with bodies from a place in Serbia to Batajnica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, yes. I just can't be certain whether he took it all the way to Batajnica or somewhere in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know how many drivers who transported bodies you took statements from? You said one is Protic. One is Ursuljanovic. How many more?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I can't remember. But at any rate, all of the statements taken were forwarded to the district prosecutor in Negotin, interviews from -- records on all interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. You seem to indicate to me that you spoke with other drivers. You're saying you can't recall that now?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember their names, but it's true that we talked to other drivers as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... how many --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: When I say "drivers" -- I can't be certain, but when I say "drivers," that doesn't mean that all of the drivers drove corpses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's what I asked you, how many persons who transported corpses you or your working group spoke with.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: I can't be certain. I can't be positive about that, but all statements are in the case file.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you tell us about how many?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you remember Ursuljanovic's first name or given name?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you take a statement personally?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure, because the working group changed. That is to say all of us were in the working group, but depending on the tasks that needed to be performed people were added to it. At any rate, the head of the working group was Captain Dragan Karleusa. He was informed about everything, and he was the one who decided on the composition of the working group.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But were you involved at any stage in taking that statement from him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember specifically whether it was myself or some other member of the working group, but I know that a statement was taken from Ursuljanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you repeat that name, please? I think we have it Ursuljanovic. Is that the name of the person?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: Ursuljanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So the given same is Ursul. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: No, his last name is Urusuljanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. Now, did he tell you who instructed him to go and collect the bodies?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I've already told you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You don't know if he told you who told him to go and collect the bodies?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't be certain because it's been six years.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, wasn't it Protic who told you first -- well, let me ask you in an open way. Can you recall whether or not it was Protic who told you about the bodies at Batajnica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you were involved in taking a statement from Protic in 2002, can you recall if he told you that he was given a number, a Belgrade number, and he was instructed to call that number to get instructions as to where to take the bodies?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: Right now I can't remember the details from the statement given by Protic. I told you at the outset that it wasn't myself who took a statement from him in 2002 but, rather, members of the operations team, and I ordered the head of the operations team to take a statement from him in the appropriate form and to have him respond to the summons given by the OTP investigators and by the District Court in Belgrade. So I can't provide any further information about the content of his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The pits that Protic took you to at Petrovo Selo, were they on or in a MUP compound?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see in paragraph 9 of your statement you said it was near the MUP training centre in Petrovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The pits were not on premises that was under the control of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: I can't give you that information. All I know is that those pits were not within the compound of the MUP training centre in Petrovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. So you don't know whether it was on premises controlled by the MUP. But did you have to drive through the MUP training centre in Petrovo Selo to get to where these pits were if you were travelling by vehicle?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC
utterances.text: One doesn't need to go through the centre of that place. There's another road that one can take to go straight to the pits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, I wonder if we could return to this tomorrow and we could interrupt you at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Because I also understood that you should be able to clarify the position in relation to the eighth motion to amend the 65 ter list. Are you able to tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I thought I would have been -- I thought the indication was that it would be tomorrow. I think had I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, informally later Mr. Hannis indicated that he should be able to do so before today's -- close of today's proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I could not point directly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You haven't heard any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I know that most of them, many of them we would object to for a variety of reason but I could not identify the individual exhibits just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What we can do, then, at the moment is deal with the ninth motion. There is no objection from the Prosecution, we understand, to that motion to amend the 65 ter list, so we will grant it. So far as the eighth motion is concerned, we do expect to hear later this afternoon -- sorry, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We expect we shall hear later this afternoon rather than tomorrow and, therefore, we should be able to indicate informally what the decision will be, possibly even file a decision but certainly give you a statement at least of that decision tomorrow morning first thing. Mr. Furdulovic, I'm afraid we have to bring our proceedings for the day to an end at this stage because another case occupies this courtroom this afternoon. That means you will have to return here tomorrow morning at 9.00 to continue your evidence. Meanwhile, between now and then, it is absolutely vital you have no communication with anybody at all about any aspect of the evidence relating to this case. Now, would you please leave the courtroom with the usher, and we will see you tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 2nd day of April, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
